```

```

It's a generated artifact that every `entire agent add pi` will rewrite, so it'll churn against whatever CLI version each person has installed. Gitignoring it and letting `entire agent add pi` generate it per-clone would avoid that — but that's entiredb's call, not something I'd change from here.

Claude Code has a drift check that pi lacks. Let me compare.

## Immediate unblock

`--force` once, from entiredb:

```
! cd /Users/soph/Work/entire/devenv/entiredb && entire agent add pi --force
```

That's a one-time cost. After it, the file carries the `Auto-generated by...` header, and `InstallHooks` (`pi/hooks.go:76-85`) will silently rewrite it on any future content change — marker present + content differs → falls through to the write. So nobody hits this error again on that repo.

## But the real problem your constraint exposes

Committing the file makes staleness the failure mode, and **nothing detects it for pi**.

`PiAgent.AreHooksInstalled` (`pi/hooks.go:113`) only checks that the marker substring is present. It never compares against what the current template would write. So a committed extension that's marked-but-years-old reads as perfectly healthy forever — and `fireHook` swallows every error by design (`catch {}` / best-effort), so a broken extension is silent. That's exactly your "forgetting it means losing sessions", except worse: nobody forgot anything, and there's no signal.

This is already what happened in entiredb. The committed file imports `@mariozechner/pi-coding-agent`, which pi renamed to `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent`. If that fails to resolve, no hooks fire, `entire status` still reports pi hooks installed.

Claude Code is the only agent that handles this — `CheckHookConfig` returns `HooksAbsent`/`HooksCurrent`/`HooksOutdated` (`claudecode/hooks.go:470`), surfaced in `status.go:202,806` and `doctor.go:444`. And the status JSON field is already plural and general:

```go
// status.go:739
HooksOutdated []string `json:"hooks_outdated,omitempty"`
```

It's just only ever populated with `"claude-code"`. Pi and OpenCode both use the marker-only check and never appear there.

Give pi a `CheckHookConfig` equivalent and append `"pi"` to that existing `HooksOutdated` slice. One wrinkle: comparing full content breaks for local-dev installs, since `renderExtension(localDev)` substitutes `go run …` vs `entire` — a dev would show permanent false drift against the committed production file. Cleaner to stamp a template version into the header line and compare that, since it's identical across both renders:

```
// Auto-generated by `entire enable --agent pi` (template v3)
```

Then `entire status` in a fresh entiredb clone with a stale committed extension says so, and points at `entire agent add pi --force`.

Want me to build that? It's contained — the pi check plus wiring into the two existing call sites in status/doctor. OpenCode has the identical gap and could ride along, though its `InstallHooks` has no foreign-file guard at all so it silently self-heals on overwrite.

I dropped the version-stamp idea from my earlier proposal. Comparing exact content against both renders (`renderExtension(false)` and `renderExtension(true)`) is strictly better: it catches *any* template edit automatically, with no version constant anyone can forget to bump. `LocalDevHookScript` is a fixed const, so matching either render is exact and machine-independent — that's what keeps local-dev installs from reading as permanent false drift.

$ entire status   # in entiredb
  Agents · Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi
  ! Claude Code hooks out of date · run 'entire enable --force'
  ! OpenCode hooks out of date · run 'entire enable --force'

It didn't — the pre-`--force` file lacked the marker entirely, so `AreHooksInstalled` returned false and pi wasn't listed at all. The false-healthy window is the one that opens *after* the marker is present, which is where the file sits now and what the drift check covers.

The caveat: drift is measured against the checking binary's template. With a committed extension and a team on mixed CLI versions, whoever runs the newest CLI sees the warning until someone re-runs `--force` and commits. That's the correct signal for your setup — the committed file should track the newest template — but it does mean a yellow line rather than silence during version skew.

Here's what I found. The short version: **the user's diagnosis is right, but `--older-than` treats the symptom — we already have the machinery to fix this properly, and it's gated one condition too narrowly.**

## 1. Why Codex sessions never end

Codex is the only agent we integrate that has no session-end hook. It exposes `SessionStart`, `UserPromptSubmit` (→ TurnStart), `Stop` (→ **TurnEnd**, not session end), and `PreToolUse`/`PostToolUse`. Documented in `cmd/entire/cli/agent/codex/AGENT.md:197`. Every other agent maps something to `agent.SessionEnd` except `pi`.

So when someone quits Codex, no `EventSessionStop` ever fires and the state file sits there with `EndedAt == nil`.

## 2. We already handle this — for a different shape of the same problem

There's a process-liveness path built exactly for "agent went away without firing a stop hook":

- `captureSessionOwner` (`strategy/manual_commit_hooks.go:2425`) records a PID + start-time + boot + host fingerprint on **every turn start**.
- `proclive.Check` reports alive/dead/unknown against that fingerprint.
- `finalizeExitedSessions` (`session_finalize.go`) sweeps dead-owner sessions and ends them exactly as a clean stop would (PhaseEnded + eager condense). It runs automatically inside `entire status`, `entire status --json`, and `entire doctor`.

## 3. The actual bug

`State.OwnerExited()` at `session/state.go:519` early-returns false unless `Phase.IsActive()` — and `IsActive()` means only `PhaseActive`.

A Codex session that finished its last turn is in **`PhaseIdle`** (TurnEnd transitions ACTIVE → IDLE). So the dead-owner sweep skips precisely the sessions Codex leaves behind. `doctor`'s `classifySession` (`doctor.go:225`) has the same shape — it handles `IsActive()` and `PhaseEnded`, and `default: return nil` at line 277 drops IDLE on the floor.

Net effect: the session lingers in `entire status` and the `session stop` picker until `StaleSessionThreshold` (7 days) makes `StateStore.Load` **delete the file outright** — a purge, not a condense, so any pending checkpoint work is silently dropped.

`IsStuckActive()` (the 1-hour heuristic) has the same `IsActive()` gate, which is why nothing even flags them as stale.

## 4. What I'd propose

**Primary fix:** let the dead-owner sweep cover IDLE sessions too. Process death is unambiguous and instant — strictly better than any time threshold. No 3-day wait, no risk of killing a session that's merely been sitting idle in an open terminal. It's a small change to `OwnerExited()` plus the `doctor` classification, and it's reversible: `transitionFromEnded` on TurnStart clears `EndedAt` and goes ACTIVE, so a resumed session recovers.

**Still worth adding `--older-than` as a secondary escape hatch,** because liveness returns Unknown in real cases: Windows (`proclive/proc_other.go` returns `errUnsupported`), sessions recorded on another host, and legacy sessions with no `Owner`. Cheap to build — `dispatch.ParseSinceAtNow` already parses `3d`, `2 days ago`, and ISO dates.

**Available today as a workaround:** `entire session stop --all --force` — but it's indiscriminate, it'd stop a live Claude session too.

Two things I'd want your call on:

- Should the IDLE sweep condense pending work (what `endSessionNow` does today) or just mark ended? Condensing is what a real SessionEnd hook would do, but it means `entire status` can now write checkpoint data as a side effect for a class of session it previously left alone.
- Is the 7-day `IsStale` hard-delete a separate bug worth filing? It discards uncondensed checkpoints rather than condensing them first.

## SessionEnd now exists

`codex-rs/hooks/schema/generated/session-end.command.input.schema.json` is there, and `HookEventName::SessionEnd` is in the protocol enum. Added 2026-07-17 in `7bd44085e1` ("Add SessionEnd hooks for thread teardown", #33895), first tagged in `rust-v0.146.0-alpha.3`.

**Your installed codex-cli is 0.147.0, so you already have it.**

It fires from `core/src/session/handlers.rs:611`, at the very end of shutdown — after `conversation.shutdown()`, task aborts, MCP teardown. Codex calls `flush_rollout()` immediately before firing (`hook_runtime.rs:396`), so the transcript is complete when our hook reads it. It's root-session-only; subagent sessions are skipped in favour of `SubagentStop`.

## Hooks are no longer feature-gated

`Feature::CodexHooks` is `stage: Stage::Stable, default_enabled: true` (`codex-rs/features/src/lib.rs:1062`). Marked stable 2026-04-23 (#19012); the config key was aliased from `codex_hooks` to plain `hooks` on 2026-05-01 (#20522). Our AGENT.md's "must be enabled via `--enable codex_hooks`" is wrong on both counts.

## The catch: a hard 3-second cap

```rust
pub(crate) const SESSION_END_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SEC: u64 = 1;
/// Keep below app-server's in-process `SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT`
pub(crate) const SESSION_END_MAX_TIMEOUT_SEC: u64 = 3;
```

`normalize_command_hook` (`engine/discovery.rs:641`) clamps SessionEnd to `[1, 3]` seconds and warns if you ask for more — every other event keeps the 600s default. And since `dd916428cd` (#37527) codex **terminates the timed-out hook's whole process tree**.

That's a real problem for us: `endSessionNow` marks ended *and* eagerly condenses. Condensation over a large rollout will blow past 3s and get killed mid-flight. So we can't just wire SessionEnd to the existing handler — the codex path needs to write the ended state first (cheap, sub-100ms) and get the condense off the critical path, leaving PostCommit to retry.

Payload is also thinner than the others: `session_id`, `cwd`, `transcript_path`, `hook_event_name`, and `reason` — which is the const `"other"`, so no clear/exit/logout distinction. No `model`, no `permission_mode`, no `turn_id`. And there's no `.output.schema.json` at all, so stdout is ignored; only the exit code counts.

## Also new since we last looked

- **`SubagentStart` / `SubagentStop`** — PreTask/PostTask equivalents now exist, with `agent_id`, `agent_type`, `agent_transcript_path`. AGENT.md's "No subagent hooks" is stale.
- **`PreCompact` / `PostCompact`** and **`PermissionRequest`**.
- **PreToolUse is no longer shell-only** — it's generic through the tool registry (`tools/registry.rs:569`), with payloads implemented for shell, `apply_patch`, MCP tools, and unified_exec.

Full hooks.json event set is now 11: PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, PostToolUse, PreCompact, PostCompact, SessionStart, SessionEnd, UserPromptSubmit, SubagentStart, SubagentStop, Stop (`config/src/hook_config.rs:36`).

## What this does to the plan

The root cause is now fixable at source rather than worked around — register the SessionEnd hook and Codex sessions end like every other agent's.

I'd still fix the IDLE gap in `OwnerExited()` though, as defense in depth. It covers three cases SessionEnd won't: users on codex < 0.146, a crashed or `kill -9`'d codex where teardown never runs, and the 3s timeout case where our own hook gets killed before it writes.

That makes `--older-than` the weakest of the three, and probably not worth building — it'd only serve Windows (`proclive` is unsupported there) and cross-host session states.

One thing I did *not* verify: AGENT.md claims `codex exec` fires no lifecycle hooks, which shapes the whole `entire review` integration. The hooks engine is constructed in `core/src/session/mod.rs`, shared by both TUI and exec, so that may have changed too — but I'd want to test it empirically before we rely on it.

## What shipped

**1. Root cause — `fix(session)`.** `OwnerExited()` gated on `Phase.IsActive()`, which is only `PhaseActive`. An agent that finishes its last turn goes ACTIVE→IDLE, so a session whose agent then quit was invisible to the dead-owner sweep. Now only already-finalized sessions are excluded. `doctor`'s `classifySession` checks it ahead of the phase switch for the same reason.

**2. The real fix — `feat(codex)`.** Registered Codex's SessionEnd hook. Hook timeouts became per-event, since SessionEnd is clamped to 3s while everything else keeps 30s, and the command match now includes the timeout so hooks installed by an older Entire get rewritten instead of nagging at every startup. The new `agent.SessionEndBudgeter` bounds only the eager condense — mark-ended stays unbounded so a session can never be left un-finalized.

**3. `fix(status)`** — a leak my change would have made common: the sweep's `phase transition` line printed raw onto the terminal mid-`entire status`, because neither `status` nor `doctor` initializes logging and `slog.Default()` writes to stderr. Now routed to `.entire/logs/`, initialized lazily only when there's actually something to finalize.

|---|---|---|

| `entire status` | lists it under **Active Sessions** | nothing lingering |

That path is what covers codex < 0.146 and killed agents.

**The `--older-than` flag isn't in here.** Once process-death handles it automatically, the flag only serves Windows (`proclive` is unsupported there) and cross-host state. Say the word if you still want it as an escape hatch.

**`codex exec` now fires hooks — which undercuts an assumption `entire review` is built on.** All five fire, and with `ENTIRE_REVIEW_*` set the session *is* tagged `kind: agent_review` with skills and prompt captured. But **no hooks fire under `-s read-only`**, and `buildCodexReviewCmd` passes no `-s` flag — so whether a review yields a tagged session depends on the user's default sandbox. The `run.Buffer` fallback is still required. I documented this and flagged it as follow-up rather than reworking review inside a session-cleanup fix; it needs its own testing.

## Blocking: the refs OPF walk infers "unpushed" from the trailer; the v1 walk asks the remote

The two rewrites use **different definitions of the boundary**, and only one is safe.

`RewriteUnpushedV1WithOPF` reads the remote tip, computes a merge-base, **aborts with `V1DivergedError`** if the remote isn't an ancestor, and bounds the walk at `remoteTip` — so it only ever rewrites genuinely unpushed commits.

`RewriteQueuedCheckpointRefsWithOPF` reads no remote at all, by explicit design: *"Discovery is the push-discovery queue rather than a local-vs-remote diff… so there is no merge-base or divergence analysis."* Its boundary is `unappliedAncestry`, which walks back until it hits a commit carrying `Entire-OPF-Applied`.

Those agree only if trailer-presence ⇔ pushed-ness. They diverge exactly when a commit was pushed **without** the trailer — OPF was off then, the user chose `OPFSkip`, or OPF was enabled later. In that case the walk goes straight past the pushed commit and rewrites it.

Reachability is ordinary, not exotic: `setRef` enqueues on *every* write to a checkpoint's ref (its own comment: *"only its remote sync is missed until a later write to the same checkpoint re-enqueues it"*), and second writes are routine — multi-session checkpoints, transcript backfill, the finalize rewrite. So "pushed once pre-OPF, written again post-OPF" is the normal shape.

Consequence chain: rewriting a pushed commit makes the push non-fast-forward → `pushCheckpointRefWithRecovery` fetch+replays → the remote **keeps the original 8-layer commit and gains the rewritten one**. Rewriting cannot un-push. The tip then carries `Entire-OPF-Applied: true`, so the user believes the ref is 9-layer throughout. That's precisely the outcome `V1DivergedError` exists to prevent on the other path.

Secondary effect: the refs path applies `BootstrapTooLargeError` per-ref unconditionally, while v1 applies it only when `remoteTip.IsZero()`. So the first push after enabling OPF can fail per-ref for a reason the v1 path wouldn't produce.

You're right to push, and the second question exposes that my framing was wrong. Two separate things:

**Enabling OPF alone picks up nothing.** Discovery is the push queue, and an already-pushed ref isn't in it — the queue is drained on flush. So enablement by itself re-processes nothing. The trigger is a **subsequent write to that same checkpoint**, because `setRef` → `enqueueForPush` runs unconditionally on every write ("only its remote sync is missed until a later write to the same checkpoint re-enqueues it"). My "enabling OPF later" phrasing implied enablement was the trigger. It isn't, and that matters — it makes the precondition much narrower than I made it sound.

**Why the pushed commit is in the walk at all**: `refBase` returns the existing ref tip as the new commit's parent, so a second write is *parented onto* the first. `unappliedAncestry` then walks first-parents from the new tip and stops only at a commit carrying `Entire-OPF-Applied`. The already-pushed commit has no trailer, so the walk doesn't stop — it continues past it, to the root.

So the full precondition is: OPF off (or `OPFSkip`) → checkpoint written → **pushed** → OPF on (or `Run`) → same checkpoint written again (attach, transcript backfill/finalize rewrite, or a second session condensing into it) → next push. That's narrow. The `OPFSkip` variant is the more reachable one, since Skip is a per-push choice and the prompt default is "ask".

**And my stated consequence was overstated.** I led with "the user believes 9-layer while 8-layer content remains on the remote." That's not fair: content pushed while OPF was off or skipped was 8-layer by the user's own configuration, and enabling OPF later makes no retroactive promise about what's already published. There's no new leak. Withdraw the privacy framing, and with it the "blocking" severity.

What's actually left is a robustness/consistency issue:

- OPF inference re-runs over already-pushed commits, and those bytes count toward `OPFBatchTooLargeError` / `OPFRawBytesTooLargeError` / `BootstrapTooLargeError` — so a push can fail closed for reasons unrelated to the content being pushed.
